title: Addresses and indirection
goal: Choose a live object by its address and update it through a pointer while keeping the other object unchanged.

prerequisites.text: You will use int variables, an if statement and the lifetime of a local variable.

terms.title: Object
terms.definition: Storage in which a value is held. The object value in the example starts with the integer 8.

terms.title: Pointer
terms.definition: An object whose value can point to another object. The pointer p and the integer value have separate storage.

terms.title: Indirection
terms.definition: The expression *p denotes the object targeted by p when the pointer is valid for that access.

sections.title: Choose a counter, then update it
paragraphs: Two counters need the same increment. A pointer lets the program select a counter first and then use one shared assignment.

In the declaration int *p, the asterisk is part of the declaration of a pointer. The expression *p dereferences p and accesses the object it points to. &value computes the address of the live variable value, which p stores after assignment.
Before access, establish which live object the pointer targets. In the example the initial assignment proves it. In the exercise the selection is checked before dereferencing.

sections.title: One write and two ways to read it
paragraphs: Predict both output numbers. The stored integer changes and p continues to point to the same object.
steps: The declaration of value creates an object holding 8.
&value computes its address, which p stores.
*p += 3 reads the integer in value and writes 11 back to that object.
trace: p has yet to be declared

sections.title: Use the address of the selected object
paragraphs: Clang rejects int *p = value in the separate diagnostic. The expression value has type int. Use &value to obtain its address.
When there is no selection, the exercise returns before reading or writing through selected. Check the two printed numbers to confirm that exactly one counter changed.

sections.title: Try the model on a different pair
paragraphs: Suppose the left counter is 20, the right counter is −1 and the increment is 5. For selection 2, write down where selected points, then predict both outputs.

reading.author: ISO/IEC JTC1/SC22/WG14
reading.title: ISO/IEC 9899:2018 — Programming languages — C
reading.purpose: Check object lifetime and the rules for & and *.

selfcheck.prompt: Which expression reads the integer 11 through p after the update?
Memory locations may vary between runs. How can you check the update?
options: Check the numeric spelling of the address
feedback: The numeric appearance of an address is unnecessary.
Use *p to check the integer stored in the object.

selfcheck.prompt: With selection 1 and counters 20 and −1, what is printed after adding 5? Why does the right number stay the same?
selfcheck.feedback: The output is 25 -1. selected holds the address of the left counter, so the one write through *selected affects that counter.

practice.title: Increment the selected counter
practice.task: The left counter starts at 4 and the right at 10. Read a selection integer from the first line. Select the left counter for 1 and the right counter for 2. Add 3 through a pointer and print the two counters in their original order, separated by a space. Print invalid for any other selection or malformed input. Use the supplied read_integer. Ignore subsequent lines.
practice.hint: Trace the assignment to selected in the branch for 2. Then establish which object the shared *selected += 3 updates.
criteria: An invalid selection outputs only invalid and returns before dereferencing.
The update uses one shared write through selected.

steps.action: Open Practice with input 2. Select Run my code.
steps.why: Compare the selected object with the two output values.
steps.expected: The starter prints 7 10. Selection 2 should print 4 13.

steps.action: Fix the address in the branch for 2 and run again.
steps.why: One shared update should affect the selected object.
Check the other branch and rejection before access.
steps.expected: The outputs are 7 10, invalid and invalid in order.

exercises.title: Independent transfer
exercises.task: Save a copy of your corrected main.c in a separate text file. Set the counters to 20 and -1 and the increment to 5. Predict and verify the result for selection 2, then restore your exercise code.
criteria: The output 20 4 preserves the left counter and updates the right counter.
